This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In the PCA on the twelve forms of capital in hundred-year time slices, PC1 (31.8% of variance; high values = greater accumulation of capital, loading positively on copper/gold, pottery decoration, depots, hatchets/swords, daggers, monument size, house size and monument count, negatively on pottery form diversity, axes/celts and amber) reaches its maximum of the entire 4300-500 BCE series at the beginning of the Younger Bronze Age, 1100 BCE (PC1 = 4.45). All subsequent horizons 1000-500 BCE have markedly lower PC1 values (mean 1.44, range 0.82-2.17), i.e. roughly 3 PC1 units (~1.6 SD) lower, with an abrupt drop at 1000 BCE and a further near-monotonic decline to 500 BCE. The gap is driven mainly by social capital (copper/gold, monument count), then symbolic (house size, daggers) and economic capital (depots), while cultural capital (pottery decoration) slightly counteracts it. The direction is robust to correlation-based PCA, a PCA fit only on the YBA slices, and the time_series_data.csv raw points.

sub_hypo.text: PC1 explains 31.8% of variance in the twelve forms of capital, with higher values indicating greater capital accumulation.
sub_hypo.context: Centered PCA of twelve Z variables in 39 hundred-year slices spanning 4300–500 BCE; PC1 oriented so its loading sum is positive.
sub_hypo.relations: PC1 loads positively on copper/gold, pottery decoration, depots, hatchets/swords, daggers, monument size, house size and monument count, and negatively on pottery form diversity, axes/celts and amber. No loading direction is specified for sickles.

sub_hypo.text: PC1 reaches its maximum of the entire 4300–500 BCE series at 1100 BCE, the beginning of the Younger Bronze Age, with a score of 4.45.
sub_hypo.context: PCA on twelve forms of capital in 39 hundred-year slices spanning 4300–500 BCE.
sub_hypo.relations: The derived PC1 score at 1100 BCE is 4.45 and exceeds the score at every other time slice.

sub_hypo.text: All horizons from 1000–500 BCE have markedly lower PC1 scores than 1100 BCE, with an abrupt drop at 1000 BCE followed by a further near-monotonic decline to 500 BCE.
sub_hypo.context: Comparison of 1100 BCE against subsequent hundred-year horizons from 1000–500 BCE in the capital PCA.
sub_hypo.relations: Subsequent PC1 scores average 1.44 and range from 0.82 to 2.17, roughly 3 PC1 units or 1.6 SD below the 1100 BCE score of 4.45; scores drop abruptly at 1000 BCE and then decline nearly monotonically toward 500 BCE.

sub_hypo.text: The PC1 gap between 1100 BCE and 1000–500 BCE is driven mainly by social capital, followed by symbolic and economic capital, while cultural capital slightly counteracts the gap.
sub_hypo.context: Variable-wise contributions to the PC1 difference between 1100 BCE and the subsequent 1000–500 BCE horizons, grouped by capital type.
sub_hypo.relations: Social capital (copper/gold and monument count) contributes most to the gap, followed by symbolic capital (house size and daggers) and economic capital (depots). Cultural capital (pottery decoration) contributes slightly in the opposite direction.

sub_hypo.text: The direction of the PC1 difference is robust to correlation-based PCA, PCA fitted only to Younger Bronze Age slices, and PCA on raw time-series points.
sub_hypo.context: Robustness checks using correlation PCA, PCA restricted to seven Younger Bronze Age slices, and PCA on 37 raw points in time_series_data.csv.
sub_hypo.relations: The direction of higher PC1 at 1100 BCE than in subsequent 1000–500 BCE horizons persists across the alternative PCA specifications and raw-point analysis.

native_result.query: In the PCA conducted on forms of capital, analyzed in hundred-year time slices, how are the symbolic capital components such as house size, daggers, and hatchets/swords characterized in terms of their values on the first principal component (PC1) and distribution across the second principal component (PC2)?
native_result.HypoA: Symbolic capital components such as house size, the number of daggers, and hatchets/swords are characterized by negative values on the first principal component (PC1) and exhibit a wide distribution of values on the second principal component (PC2). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In the PCA of the 12 forms of capital over 39 hundred-year bins (4300-500 BCE), the symbolic-capital variables house size, daggers and hatchets/swords all have moderate positive loadings on PC1 (0.23-0.30; correlations 0.44-0.58), lying on the same side of PC1 as copper/gold, pottery decoration and depots and opposite to pottery form, axes/celts, amber and sickles; PC1 (30% variance) tracks the Neolithic-to-Bronze-Age chronology. On PC2 (19.5%) the three symbolic items are dispersed rather than clustered: daggers (0.07) and hatchets/swords (0.05) sit near zero, whereas house size (0.33) loads clearly higher, near monument size/count, amber and axes/celts. Hence symbolic capital is characterized by consistently moderate, same-sign PC1 values and a spread-out, non-uniform distribution across PC2.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read data/capital.csv with decimal=','; dropped group/color; 12 Z variables x 39 bins (already 100-yr spacing, no NaN). Correlation PCA (center+unit scale) via numpy SVD; sign fixed so each PC's loading sum is positive. Reported explained variance, eigenvector and correlation loadings for PC1/PC2 with capital-type labels, 39 scores with group-wise summary, PC1-PC2 biplot (SVG). Sensitivity: covariance PCA (no rescale, ZSichel std 0.54 noted), dropping duplicate 4300/4200 BCE rows (n=37), time_series_data raw Z (identical to capital.csv, 37 bins) and 100-yr bin means of _inter columns; relative positions of the three symbolic variables were stable in all runs.

native_result.HypoA: Amber has historically high and stable values in the 4th millenium BCE. with its all time peak around 3300 to 3000BCE.
native_result.HypoB: Amber (Z-standardised value) was highest in the 4th millennium BCE (4000–3001 BCE, mean Z = 1.48; all bins 1.46–1.54), and peaked in the interval 3300–3000 BCE (Middle Neolithic), where it reached its maximum Z = 1.54 across four consecutive 100-year bins, at the end of a broader high phase (Z ≥ 1.46) from 4000 to 3000 BCE; it then fell sharply to 0.37 at 2900 BCE and to negative values from 2700 BCE onward. The 3000 BCE bin lies on the millennium boundary, but the 4th millennium remains highest under either boundary convention.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded capital.csv (decimal-comma Zamber, 39 bins 4300–500 BCE, 100-yr step) and time_series_data.csv (Amber at 100-yr anchors, Amber_inter yearly); merged on CE=-BCE and verified 0 mismatches in 37 shared bins. Assigned each 100-yr bin to a millennium under two conventions (4000–3001 BCE; and 4000–3000 BCE inclusive), computed mean/max/min per millennium, located the global-maximum plateau and the Z>=1.46 high phase, inspected the post-plateau drop, and verified Amber_inter gives the same maximum (1.54, CE -3300..-3000). Tables saved to output/.

native_result.HypoB: Summed social capital (Z CopperGold + Z Amber + Z MonumentCount) peaked in the 1400 BCE century bin (Older Bronze Age), value 4.24, holding as a plateau through 1300 BCE. Entering the peak (1400 vs 1500 BCE) all three components increased: Copper and Gold rose most (+2.90, to 2.54), Monument Count rose strongly (+1.54, to 1.71), and Amber rose only slightly (+0.14, to -0.01, still below average). The peak is driven by copper/gold and monuments, not amber; in 1200-1100 BCE copper/gold reached its all-time maximum (2.85) but amber and monuments declined, lowering the sum to 3.62, and by 1000 BCE it collapsed (-1.43). A secondary peak at 2700 BCE (2.96) was due solely to monument count.

native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs strongly among habitat types (Kruskal-Wallis H=140.7, df=9, p=7e-26; Poisson GLM LRT p=2e-37). It is highest in human-modified, low-elevation and water-associated habitats - Coastal (0.79 species/plot, 45% of plots invaded), Wetlands (0.76, 50%), Urban (0.69, 48%) and Riparian (0.57, 36%), ~30-42x the rate in Scrublands - intermediate in Croplands (0.22/plot, 21%, ~11.5x; non-natives there are mainly unintentional), and near zero in natural/semi-natural habitats: Meadows (0.10, 8%), Coniferous forests (0.09, 6%), Broad-leaved forests (0.06, 4%), Scrublands (0.02, 2%) and Rock outcrops (0 of 57 plots). The habitat effect remains significant after adjusting for elevation, urban/cropland cover and distance to road (LRT p=1.5e-12), though attenuated (adjusted RR ~24-25x), with elevation an additional negative predictor.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read invaded_niche_pathways.csv (tab-separated, 632 plots x 37 cols, no NA; row=plot assumed from unique lon/lat). Primary measure per-plot n.gard, secondary presence (n.gard>0), tertiary share n.gard/n.total (reported only). Per-habitat summaries with Wilson/exact Poisson CIs; Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests; Poisson GLM n.gard~habitat (Pearson chi2/df 1.14-1.25, NB2 check gave identical rate ratios); Rock outcrops (0/57 events, complete separation) excluded from regression and reported descriptively; rate ratios vs Scrublands; adjusted Poisson adding elevation, urban.2009.500m, cropland.2009.500m, distance.road for robustness; grouped high/mid/low contrasts via Mann-Whitney. Code: analysis/gardening_by_habitat.py; output: analysis/output.txt.

native_result.HypoB: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs strongly among habitat types (NB GLM LR chi2=148.4, df=9, p=1.9e-27). Per plot, gardening species are most numerous in lowland anthropogenic/wet habitats — Coastal (0.79 species/plot, 95% CI 0.49–1.30), Wetlands (0.76, 0.49–1.18), Urban (0.69, 0.49–0.98) and Riparian (0.57, 0.39–0.84), which do not differ from each other — intermediate in Croplands (0.22; 3.2x lower than Urban, Holm p=0.003), and nearly absent in Meadows (0.10), Coniferous forests (0.09), Broad-leaved forests (0.06), Scrublands (0.02) and Rock outcrops (0/57 plots); the rich group has ~14x more gardening species per plot than the forest/scrub/rock group (0.68 vs 0.05). Where the denominator is adequate (>=40 non-native records), the gardening share of all non-native species is highest in Wetlands (29/52 = 56%) and Coastal (23/43 = 53%), lower in Riparian (35/96 = 36%) and Urban (45/151 = 30%, dominated by unintentional introductions), and lowest in Croplands (20/108 = 19%) (binomial LR chi2=50.6, p=8e-8; pooled chi2=75.2, Monte-Carlo p=1e-4). The habitat effect persists after adjusting for elevation, urban cover (500 m) and log distance to road (LR chi2=67.5, df=9, p=5e-11), although elevation explains part of it (-1.93 per km, p<1e-4): habitats rich in gardening species are low-elevation and closer to roads/built-up areas, an observed correlation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/invaded_niche_pathways.csv (tab-separated; 632 plots, 10 habitats; verified n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo==n.total for all rows). Main model: n.gard ~ habitat, negative binomial (NB2) fitted by ML with statsmodels (BFGS; Newton/IRLS failed because Rock outcrops has 0 events), Poisson as control (AIC 695.9 vs NB 688.0; alpha=0.56, boundary LR p=0.0009; NB reproduces 514.4 expected vs 515 observed zeros, so ZINB not used). Reference level Urban. LR test habitat vs intercept-only, delta-method predicted means with 95% CI, 45 pairwise log-rate-ratio contrasts with Holm correction, grouped rich/Croplands/poor NB model, Kruskal-Wallis check. Secondary: binomial GLM of n.gard/(n.total) ~ habitat on 191 plots with n.total>0 (Pearson dispersion 0.98), Wilson CIs on pooled shares. Cross-check: chi-square on pooled 10x3 habitat x pathway table with Monte-Carlo p (20000 fixed-margin simulations) due to 17/30 expected cells <5, plus restricted (>=10 records) and 10x2 versions. Sensitivity: NB with elevation (km), urban.2009.500m and log(distance.road); LR tests of habitat given covariates and vice versa; AIC comparison. Packages: pandas 3.0.2, numpy, scipy.stats, statsmodels 0.14.6. Species-level file and phylogeny not used (no per-species habitat).

native_result.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: La prevalencia de plantas no nativas de jardinería varía fuertemente con el hábitat (Poisson LRT χ²=196, df=9, p≈2e-37): es máxima en hábitats húmedos y antropizados —costeros (0.79 esp./parcela, 45% presencia), humedales (0.76, 50%), urbanos (0.69, 48%) y ribereños (0.57, 36%)—, intermedia en cultivos (0.22, 21%) y casi nula en pastos (0.10), bosques de coníferas (0.09), bosques caducifolios (0.06), matorrales (0.02) y roquedos (0/57). Agrupado: 0.68 vs 0.22 vs 0.05 esp./parcela (~14×). Tras ajustar por urbanización, elevación y distancia a carreteras el efecto del hábitat persiste (χ²=79, p≈2e-13), el ordenamiento se mantiene (Spearman 0.90) con los cuatro hábitats húmedos/antropizados ≈0.40 vs cultivos 0.16 y ≤0.09 en naturales; Urban IRR vs cultivos 3.2→2.6; la elevación es la única covariable significativa (IRR 0.998/m), la cobertura urbana a 500 m no (p=0.37).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga de invaded_niche_pathways.csv (tab-delimitado, 632 parcelas, 10 hábitats; n.total verificado = n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo; 441 parcelas con n.total=0 conservadas). 2) Descriptivos por hábitat: media n.gard con IC95% Poisson exacto, % parcelas con n.gard>0, n.gard/n.total (solo descriptivo). 3) GLM Poisson n.gard~habitat (ref. Croplands), LRT global, chequeo de sobredispersión (Pearson, Cameron-Trivedi), confirmación con binomial negativa (excluyendo Rock outcrops, todo ceros) y SE robustos. 4) Modelo ajustado + urban.2009.500m + elevation + distance.road; medias predichas por hábitat, comparación de rangos (Spearman) y del coeficiente de Urban. 5) GLM binomial de presencia crudo y ajustado. 6) Agrupación descriptiva húmedos/antropizados vs agrícola vs naturales. 7) Moran's I (k=8, inversa distancia, permutaciones) sobre n.gard y residuos Pearson. Script: analysis/gardening_habitat_analysis.py; salida: analysis/output.txt.

native_result.HypoB: The prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening varies strongly with habitat type (Poisson GLM LRT chi2=196.1, df=9, p=2e-37). Ranking: Coastal ≈ Wetlands ≈ Urban ≈ Riparian > Croplands > Meadows ≈ Coniferous ≈ Broad-leaved ≈ Scrublands ≈ Rock outcrops. The habitat effect persists after adjusting for elevation, urban/cropland cover, and distance to roads and streams (chi2=79.5, p=2e-13), with the high-prevalence habitats having ~24–25× (unadjusted 30–42×) the rate of Scrublands.

Robustness: Kruskal-Wallis H=140.7 p=7e-26; chi-square habitat×presence chi2=139.5 p=1e-25; pairwise Fisher+Holm (24/45). native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway's prevalence differs across habitat types in the context of the elevation/climate gradient and surrounding urban land cover (500-1000 m buffer): in human-dominated habitats (Urban, Croplands) gardening prevalence is insensitive to elevation, temperature and urban cover, whereas in natural/semi-natural habitats it tracks these gradients - in Riparian and Wetland habitats the gardening share of non-native species increases with elevation (and decreasing temperature) and decreases with urban cover, while in absolute terms gardening species counts fall with elevation and rise with urban cover in Coastal, Riparian and forest/scrub/meadow habitats but not in Urban plots. (2) Proportion view: binomial GLM n.gard/n.total ~ habitat * context on 191 invaded plots, contexts tested one at a time (elevation, temperature, rainfall, radiation, urban 50/500/1000 m 2009, cropland 50/500 m 2009, log distance road/stream), LRT + dAIC for additive vs interaction, 5-level (data-rich + Other) and 10-level habitat codings, within-habitat slopes, stratified median-split Fisher checks. (3) Count view: n.gard ~ habitat * context on all 632 plots; Poisson overdispersion check (1.33), NB (alpha 0.57), ZIP and ZINB compared by AIC; NB used for LRTs with Poisson 10-level fallback. native_result.HypoB: Gardening-introduced non-native plants are prevalent only in low-elevation, human-influenced habitats of the Barcelona province (Wetlands 50% of plots, Urban 48%, Coastal 45%, Riparian 36%, Croplands 21% contain gardening species) and nearly absent (≤8%) in high-elevation natural habitats (meadows, forests, scrublands, rock outcrops); this occurrence gradient is driven mainly by elevation (OR 0.04 per km, p<0.001), with urban cover and road distance adding little. Within the invaded habitats two prevalence styles appear that are NOT explained by elevation/urbanisation/road covariates: gardening is the dominant pathway in Wetlands (56% of non-native records) and Coastal habitats (54%), but a secondary pathway behind unintentional introductions in Urban (30%), Riparian (37%) and Croplands (19%) (binomial GLM vs Urban: Wetlands +1.07, Coastal +1.12, Croplands −1.06 logits, all p≤0.003 after covariates). Shares for habitats with <10 records are not interpreted. Regionally gardening introductions grew from 18 (pre-1500) to 397 (1985–2019).
native_result.WorkflowB: Data: invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, TAB-delimited despite .csv; temporal_trends file also tab-delimited; buffer covariates are fractions 0-1 not percentages as datasets.json claims). (1) Descriptive table per habitat: mean n.gard, % plots with gardening, mean n.unint, share of gardening among records in invaded plots; chi-square habitat x pathway. (2) Absolute prevalence: Poisson and negative-binomial GLMs n.gard ~ habitat, with and without covariates (elevation, urban & cropland 2009 500 m, log distance to road/stream, rainfall, progressive landscape change 1956-2009); dispersion and zero checks; LRTs; Wald pairwise contrasts; Rock outcrops merged with Scrublands as reference where separation prevented convergence. (3) Relative prevalence: binomial GLM n.gard/n.total in 191 invaded plots, by habitat and by 3 habitat blocks, with/without covariates. (4) Parallel NB model for n.unint and gardening/unintentional IRR style index. (5) Interactions habitat x urban and habitat x elevation via LRT/AIC at 10 levels and in 3 blocks. native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: In Barcelona province, non-native plants introduced via the gardening pathway reach their highest absolute richness in low-elevation (<200 m), warm habitats—urban, coastal, wetland and riparian plots (0.57–0.79 species/plot vs ≤0.10 in high-elevation meadows, forests, scrublands and rock outcrops; NB IRR for elevation 0.46 per SD, p<0.001)—but their relative prevalence shows an opposite pattern: gardening is the dominant pathway in coastal (53%) and wetland (56%) plots, whereas in urban (30%) and cropland (19%) plots—habitats with the highest surrounding urban/cropland cover, closest to roads and the largest totals of non-native species—the alien flora is dominated by unintentional introductions (69–77%), and riparian plots are intermediate (gardening 37%, unintentional 50%, agri-forestry 13%, the highest agri-forestry share). Thus gardening is both abundant and dominant in low-elevation water-related semi-natural habitats, abundant but diluted by unintentional introductions in highly urbanised/agricultural habitats (gardening share declines with surrounding urban cover, OR≈0.81 per SD; interaction with water-related habitats p=0.036), and scarce in high-elevation natural habitats where estimates are unreliable.
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspected data (632 plots, 10 habitats, no missing, n.total==sum of pathways). Descriptive tables by habitat with bootstrap CIs for gardening share; Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests. Model A: negative-binomial GLM n.gard ~ habitat, then + environment (elevation, urban & cropland cover 2009/500 m, log distance to road/stream, progressive land-use change 1956–2009), AIC comparison, coefficient shifts. Model B: binomial GLM n.gard/n.total ~ habitat (+env) on 191 invaded plots, plus NB with offset(log n.total). Parallel summaries for n.unint and n.agfo. Sensitivity: 9 year×buffer land-use specs and climate instead of elevation. Interactions of grouped habitats (anthropogenic/water-related/natural) with environment and stratified tables. Moran's I on deviance residuals (k=8 inverse-distance, 999 permutations).

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land cover in the immediate surroundings of a plot (50 m buffer) as of 1993 promoted invasion by non-native plants introduced through the Gardening (ornamental) pathway: the count of gardening-introduced species per plot (n.gard) increases with urban.1993.50m (standardized NegBin beta ~ +0.21, 95% CI 0.03-0.38, p ~ 0.02 controlling for habitat group, climate and distance to roads/streams; GEE spatially clustered p = 0.0015), mainly by raising the probability that a plot hosts at least one gardening escape (OR 1.33 per SD). This is specific to the 1993 land-use scenario (1956 urban cover shows no or negative association; 2009 cover is weaker and non-significant after habitat control) and to the gardening pathway: the raw positive association of urban cover with unintentionally introduced species (n.unint, beta 0.3-0.44 at 500-1000 m) vanishes once anthropic habitat (urban + cropland) is controlled, and AgriForest species show no relation to urban cover at any buffer or year.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read tab-separated plot data (632 plots). Standardized urban and cropland cover per buffer (50/500/1000 m) and year (1956/1993/2009). Covariates: annual temperature, rainfall, radiation, log distance to stream and road (elevation dropped, VIF 13, r=-0.96 with temperature), and habitat under four specifications (none; 3 groups anthropic/wet/dry-forest; 10 levels; excluding Urban-habitat plots). Fitted Negative Binomial GLMs (Poisson fallback) for n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo for each of the 9 buffer x year combinations (one land-use layer per model), 108 models total; AIC used to pick best buffer-year per pathway. Checked overdispersion (Pearson chi2/df 1.08-1.18; NB AIC lower for gard/unint), hurdle decomposition (logit presence + Poisson on positives), legacy vs recent (urban1956 + delta 1956-2009), progressive/regressive 1956-2009 change, urban x habitat-group interactions (AIC), binomial compositional model of unintentional share, Moran's I on residuals (k=8 inverse-distance; raw I=0.22-0.25, residual I=0.03-0.09), GEE Poisson with 10-km grid clusters (95 clusters) for spatially robust SEs, and chi-square on the temporal contingency table (chi2=230, p=6e-47; gardening share rises from 17% to 75%).

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use promoted plant invasion specifically through the unintentional introduction pathway: per-plot richness of unintentionally introduced non-native plants in Barcelona province increases with the proportion of urban land cover around the plot (strongest for current 2009 cover at a 500 m buffer, IRR ~1.20 per +10% urban cover, p<0.001, and consistent across 50-1000 m buffers and 1956/1993/2009 years), whereas Gardening-introduced richness responds only weakly and AgriForest-introduced richness not at all (significant pathway x urban interaction, p=0.006-0.014). The effect is largely expressed in plots within urban habitat at low elevation; within non-urban habitats only a marginal positive effect of surrounding urban cover on unintentional richness remains.
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspected 4 files (632 plots, 81 species, tree tips matched). Fitted Poisson and negative-binomial GLMs of n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo on urban cover (3 years x 3 buffers, one urban + matching cropland variable per model) with covariates habitat, elevation, rainfall, log distance to road/stream; checked overdispersion, zero-inflation (observed vs expected zeros), VIFs, residual Moran's I; compared years/buffers by AIC and IRR per 10% cover; legacy (1956) vs change (2009-1956) models; stacked long-format NB with pathway x urban interaction (LR tests); habitat-adjusted vs no-habitat vs non-urban-habitat-only models; covariate-robustness sequence; binomial composition models in invaded plots; descriptive treatment of n.agfo.

native_result.query: What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use influenced the human-mediated introduction pathways: unintentional introductions most strongly and gardening (ornamental) introductions to a lesser extent, while agriculture/forestry introductions show no detectable response. Per +1 SD (~23 percentage points) of urban cover within 500 m (2009), adjusting for elevation, cropland, distance to roads/streams, rainfall and radiation, the count of unintentionally introduced non-native species per plot rises by IRR 1.39 (95% CI 1.19-1.62, p=4e-5) and gardening-introduced species by IRR 1.19 (1.01-1.39, p=0.04); AgriForest IRR 0.87 (0.62-1.23, 21 occupied plots, undetectable). The urban effect differs between unintentional and AgriForest pathways (ratio of IRRs 1.59, 1.10-2.30, p=0.013). The association is clearest at the 500 m buffer and for recent/changing urban cover (urban expansion 1956-2009: unintentional IRR 1.33, gardening 1.16), and is largely carried by plots in urban habitat (within-habitat slopes ~1.0 after adding a habitat factor).
native_result.WorkflowB: 632 plots from invaded_niche_pathways.csv. Z-scored predictors; VIF screening dropped annual.temperature (VIF 21, r=-0.96 with elevation). Per-pathway Poisson GLMs (Pearson chi2/df 0.60-1.15, so NB not required) of n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo on urban.2009.500m + elevation + cropland.2009.500m + log distance.road + log distance.stream + annual.rainfall + annual.radiation, with and without 10-level habitat; logit presence/absence for n.agfo. Stacked long-format Poisson model (1896 obs) with urban x pathway interaction and pathway-specific covariate slopes, cluster-robust SE by plot, LR test of interaction. Sensitivity across buffers (50/500/1000 m), years (1956/1993/2009), and urban-1956 + delta-urban joint model. Moran's I on Pearson residuals (k=8 NN, 999 permutations) and HC1 robust SEs. Optional binomial composition model of unintentional share among invaded plots. Phylogenetic tree not used (plot-level counts carry no species identity).

Per +1 SD (~23 percentage points) of urban cover within 500 m (2009), adjusting for elevation, cropland, distance to roads/streams, rainfall and radiation, the count of unintentionally introduced non-native species per plot rises by IRR 1.39 (95% CI 1.19-1.62, p=4e-5) and gardening-introduced species by IRR 1.19 (1.01-1.39, p=0.04); AgriForest IRR 0.87 (0.62-1.23, 21 occupied plots, undetectable). The urban effect differs between unintentional and AgriForest pathways (ratio of IRRs 1.59, 1.10-2.30, p=0.013). The association is clearest at the 500 m buffer and for recent/changing urban cover (urban expansion 1956-2009: unintentional IRR 1.33, gardening 1.16), and is largely carried by plots in urban habitat (within-habitat slopes ~1.0 after adding a habitat factor).
P0||G0.WorkflowB: 632 plots from invaded_niche_pathways.csv. Z-scored predictors; VIF screening dropped annual.temperature (VIF 21, r=-0.96 with elevation). Per-pathway Poisson GLMs (Pearson chi2/df 0.60-1.15, so NB not required) of n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo on urban.2009.500m + elevation + cropland.2009.500m + log distance.road + log distance.stream + annual.rainfall + annual.radiation, with and without 10-level habitat; logit presence/absence for n.agfo. Stacked long-format Poisson model (1896 obs) with urban x pathway interaction and pathway-specific covariate slopes, cluster-robust SE by plot, LR test of interaction. Sensitivity across buffers (50/500/1000 m), years (1956/1993/2009), and urban-1956 + delta-urban joint model. Moran's I on Pearson residuals (k=8 NN, 999 permutations) and HC1 robust SEs. Optional binomial composition model of unintentional share among invaded plots. Phylogenetic tree not used (plot-level counts carry no species identity).

native_result.HypoB: Urban land use is associated with non-native plants introduced unintentionally and, more weakly, with those introduced through gardening, but not with agriculture/forestry introductions. Negative-binomial GLMs (alpha by ML) for n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo with one urban variable per model (3 years x 3 buffers = 9 models), matching cropland, elevation, rainfall, log road/stream distance; versions without and with a 6-level habitat factor (five sparse habitats merged to avoid complete separation). Primary = urban.2009.500m. Composition: binomial share models (weights n.total, HC1) and multinomial logit on 481 records in 191 plots with n.total>0; n.total NB model. Moran's I on deviance residuals (kNN8 and inverse-distance <5 km, UTM coords); corrections via 10-km-block cluster-robust SE and quadratic spatial trend. AgriForest presence/absence logistic as robustness. Poisson vs NB AIC comparison.

native_result.query: What types of plant introductions were influenced by urban land use?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use influences non-native plant introductions that occurred unintentionally (strong, consistent positive effect on plot-level unintentional-pathway richness: NB IRR 3.2-6.3 for 0->1 urban cover, 8/9 buffer-year variants p<0.01, strongest for 1993-2009 urban cover at 50-500 m) and, more weakly and less robustly, gardening (ornamental) introductions (IRR 1.7-2.9, significant only for 1993 urban cover at 50 and 500 m), while agriculture/forestry introductions show no detectable relationship (underpowered: 21 non-zero plots). Urbanisation also shifts the pathway composition of invaded plots toward unintentional rather than gardening species (OR 0.36 for gardening share per unit urban 2009/500 m, p=0.035). Effects are estimated controlling for cropland cover, elevation, temperature, rainfall and distances to roads/streams; they are largely absorbed by habitat type (the 'Urban' habitat class), so the urban effect operates at the landscape/habitat level rather than within habitats.
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspected data (632 plots, no NA, land-use as proportions). For each pathway count (n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo) fitted Poisson and NB2 GLMs against each of 9 urban buffer x year variables, plus cropland at the same scale/year, standardized elevation, annual temperature, rainfall, log distance to road and stream, with and without 10-class habitat; chose family by AIC/dispersion; tabulated urban IRRs with 95% CI (analysis/urban_IRR_sensitivity_table.csv). Diagnostics: Pearson dispersion, simulated zero-count check for zero-inflation, Moran's I on Pearson residuals (k=10 inverse-distance weights, permutation test), spatial-trend robustness refit. Pathway comparison: binomial composition model (gardening vs other, plots with n.total>0) and long-format NB with pathway x urban interaction and cluster-robust SEs. Supplementary: coarse habitat grouping, exclusion of Urban-habitat plots, land-use intensification (progressive 1956-2009) models.

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use in the Barcelona province increased plant invasion selectively by introduction pathway: unintentionally introduced species responded most strongly (NB GLM without habitat: IRR 1.20 per +10 pp urban cover within 500 m in 2009, 95% CI 1.12-1.29, p<0.001), gardening/ornamental species weakly and marginally (IRR 1.08, 0.997-1.17, p=0.058), and agriculture/forestry species not at all (IRR 0.95, 0.75-1.19, p=0.64); the urban x pathway interaction is significant (joint Wald p<0.0001) with and without a habitat term. The positive urban effect on unintentional species is driven by recent (1956-2009) urban expansion (IRR 1.15 per +10 pp increase, p=0.026) rather than by urban cover already present in 1956 (IRR 0.91, p=0.09), and is matched in size by cropland cover (IRR 1.21), indicating a general response to anthropogenic land use. The absolute urban effect is confounded with habitat type: adding the 10-level habitat factor (incl. an 'Urban' habitat class) removes the continuous urban-cover effect for all pathways (IRRs 0.97-1.01, p>0.5), while gardening species are instead associated with Urban, riparian, wetland and coastal habitat identity (IRR 2.4-2.7 vs croplands).
native_result.WorkflowB: Data: invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, 0 NA). Cross-checked that n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo are species-per-plot counts against invasion_success_pathways.csv (sums 169/289/23 vs 163/288/21; small discrepancy from 4 duplicated taxa). Tree and contingency table not used (no land-use information). VIF screening dropped annual temperature (r=-0.96 with elevation). Fitted separate NB2 GLMs (alpha profiled by ML; IRLS used because discrete NB failed under habitat quasi-separation) for n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo vs urban cover with cropland (same buffer/year), elevation, rainfall, log distance to road and stream, with and without a 10-level habitat factor; Poisson comparison (dispersion, AIC, zero prediction); logistic presence/absence for AgriForest (21 presences). AIC grid of 3 buffers x 3 years per pathway. Legacy-vs-recent model (urban 1956 + delta 1956-2009) and 50 m change-category model (progressive/regressive vs no change, 1956 baseline). Long-format NB GLM count ~ urban x pathway with cluster-robust SE by plot and joint Wald test for pathway differences. Sensitivity excluding Urban-habitat plots (n=567). Moran's I on Pearson residuals (k=10 NN, 999 permutations). Script: analysis.py; outputs: output/results.txt, output/aic_table.csv.

The positive urban effect on unintentional species is driven by recent (1956-2009) urban expansion (IRR 1.15 per +10 pp increase, p=0.026) rather than by urban cover already present in 1956 (IRR 0.91, p=0.09), and is matched in size by cropland cover (IRR 1.21), indicating a general response to anthropogenic land use. The absolute urban effect is confounded with habitat type: adding the 10-level habitat factor (incl. an 'Urban' habitat class) removes the continuous urban-cover effect for all pathways (IRRs 0.97-1.01, p>0.5), while gardening species are instead associated with Urban, riparian, wetland and coastal habitat identity (IRR 2.4-2.7 vs croplands).

Cross-checked that n.gard/n.unint/n.agfo are species-per-plot counts against invasion_success_pathways.csv (sums 169/289/23 vs 163/288/21; small discrepancy from 4 duplicated taxa). Tree and contingency table not used (no land-use information). VIF screening dropped annual temperature (r=-0.96 with elevation). Fitted separate NB2 GLMs (alpha profiled by ML; IRLS used because discrete NB failed under habitat quasi-separation) for n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo vs urban cover with cropland (same buffer/year), elevation, rainfall, log distance to road and stream, with and without a 10-level habitat factor; Poisson comparison (dispersion, AIC, zero prediction); logistic presence/absence for AgriForest (21 presences). AIC grid of 3 buffers x 3 years per pathway. Legacy-vs-recent model (urban 1956 + delta 1956-2009) and 50 m change-category model (progressive/regressive vs no change, 1956 baseline). Long-format NB GLM count ~ urban x pathway with cluster-robust SE by plot and joint Wald test for pathway differences. Sensitivity excluding Urban-habitat plots (n=567). Moran's I on Pearson residuals (k=10 NN, 999 permutations). Script: analysis.py; outputs: output/results.txt, output/aic_table.csv.

native_result.query: How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?
native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use around plots strongly increased the invasion of introduced plants, but pathway-specifically: unintentionally introduced species responded most (species richness ~6x from 0 to 100% urban cover within 500 m, NB GLM exp(beta)=6.3, 95% CI 3.0-13.0; their share of all introduced species rose, OR=3.3), gardening species increased less (exp(beta)=2.25, CI 1.03-4.96) and lost relative share (OR=0.36), and agriculture/forestry species showed no increase (exp(beta)=0.6, CI 0.06-6.6; zero records in plots >50% urban; negative when habitat is controlled). The pathway x urban interaction is significant (LRT p=0.003) and robust across 8/9 buffer x year combinations; mean introduced richness per plot rose from 0.11 (0% urban) to 2.26 (>50% urban).
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspected 4 files (tab-separated CSVs; 632 plots, 37 vars, no NAs; 81 tree tips match phylo.tip.label). Reshaped invaded_niche_pathways.csv to long plot x pathway format (1896 rows). Fitted Poisson and negative-binomial GLMs with pathway x urban interaction, covariates cropland (same buffer/year), elevation, temperature, rainfall, log road/stream distance, with and without habitat factor; Poisson vs NB diagnostics (deviance/df, Pearson/df, LRT on alpha); pathway-specific exp(beta) with 95% CI; LRT for interaction. Sensitivity over 9 urban buffer x year predictors (AIC). Separate per-pathway NB and presence/absence logit models; model excluding 'Urban' habitat plots. Compositional binomial models of pathway share given n.total. Descriptive counts by urban cover class. Moran's I on residuals (10-NN inverse-distance weights, permutation test). Tree and temporal table used as context only. Scripts: analysis/urban_pathways_analysis.py, analysis/robustness_extra.py; output in analysis/output.txt.

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land use affected introduced plants differently by introduction pathway: plots with more surrounding urban cover held more non-native species overall (NB IRR ≈ 1.35 per SD urban cover, p < 0.001), and this was driven by unintentionally introduced species (IRR ≈ 1.44 per SD, p < 0.001), whose richness and proportional share increased with urbanisation; gardening/ornamental species responded weakly and non-significantly once elevation was controlled (IRR ≈ 1.13, p = 0.22) and their share declined with urban cover; agriculture/forestry species showed no positive response (negative slope). The pathway × urban interaction was significant (LR p = 0.027; robust Wald p = 0.004) and the ordering Unintentional > Gardening > AgriForest held across all years (1956/1993/2009) and buffer scales (50/500/1000 m). Within habitat types (i.e., after controlling for an 'Urban' habitat class) urban cover added no extra positive effect; elevation (lowlands) was the strongest predictor, and historical (1956) vs current (2009) urban cover could not be statistically separated.
native_result.WorkflowB: Data: invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots). Responses: counts n.gard, n.unint, n.total (n.agfo only 21 non-zero plots -> univariate tests only). Covariate screening: elevation~temperature r=-0.96, elevation~rainfall r=0.86 (VIF 13-21) -> kept elevation, radiation, log distance to road/stream, cropland (matched year/scale); final VIF<1.7. Habitat collapsed to 7 classes (4 low-invasion natural habitats merged, 308 plots, 18 records) to avoid complete separation; 10-class check for n.total gave identical urban coefficient. Distribution choice: Poisson dispersion 1.16-1.66; AIC Poisson>NB; NB reproduced observed zero fractions (0.815/0.765/0.681 vs 0.815/0.771/0.698); ZIP/ZINB AIC slightly lower but partly non-convergent -> negative binomial used. Main analysis: NB GLM, urban.2009.500m (per SD), with and without habitat, plus models excluding 65 Urban-habitat plots. Pathway comparison: long-format NB (632x3 rows) with pathway x urban interaction, plot-cluster-robust SE, LR and Wald tests, pathway-specific marginal slopes; repeated for 1993/500m, 2009/1000m, 1956/500m, 1956/1000m, 2009/50m. Composition: binomial share models on 191 invaded plots. History vs current: single models (2009, 1956, 1993, 1956-2009 change) compared by AIC, then joint models with VIF. Spatial: Moran's I of Pearson residuals (10-NN inverse-distance weights, 999 permutations), Moran eigenvector filtering; coefficients changed <=0.04. Key results: without habitat urban IRR n.total 1.35 (p<0.001), n.unint 1.44 (p<0.001), n.gard 1.13 (p=0.22); with habitat all urban main effects ~0 (p>0.3), elevation strongest (coef -0.76 to -0.99, p<0.001). Interaction LR chi2=7.25, p=0.027 (robust Wald p=0.004); Unintentional-Gardening slope difference +0.24 (p=0.016), Unintentional-AgriForest +0.56 (p=0.003); same ordering in all 7 year/scale fits. Share of unintentional species rises with urban (p=0.041/0.004), gardening share falls (p=0.060/0.034). History vs current: AIC differences <3, joint terms non-significant (VIF 3.7/2.2). Background: temporal_trends shows gardening introductions dominating 1985-2019 (397 species); invasion_success shows unintentional species invade more plots (median 3 vs 2).

native_result.HypoA: Urban land use reduced invasion by gardening plants over unintentionally introduced ones.
native_result.HypoB: Urban land cover around a plot increases invasion by non-native plants in a pathway-dependent way: the number of unintentionally introduced species rises most strongly with urban cover (IRR ~1.5 per +1 SD = +22.6 percentage points urban cover within 500 m, 2009), gardening introductions rise more weakly (IRR ~1.25), and agriculture/forestry introductions show no positive response (IRR ~0.8-0.94, CI includes 1; concentrated in riparian and cropland plots). Effects are driven by recent (1993/2009) urban cover; 1956 cover and 1956-2009 progressive change add no information. The decline is not specific to any one domain; between-domain differences are small and not statistically distinguishable (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.54), with relative shrinkage (rr/ro) largest in Social psychology (median 0.18) and smallest in Economics (median 0.70), the latter based on only 18 studies.

native_result.query: For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Original effect sizes tend to be larger than replication effect sizes in all three domains (Cognitive, Social, Economics; equivalently both the Psychology/rpp and Experimental Economics/ee projects): 82-88% of studies per domain have |ro|>|rr| and the mean Fisher-z difference fiso-fisr is positive and significant in each (Cognitive 0.29, Economics 0.27, Social 0.23). The absolute shrinkage does not differ across domains, but the relative shrinkage is largest in Social psychology, where replications retain only ~13-18% of the original effect (median relative_es 0.13) versus ~65-70% in Cognitive and Economics (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.015); Economics (n=18) is not reliably distinguishable from Cognitive.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded merged CSV (86 unique studies, 60 cols; no missing effect sizes, no duplicates, no incomplete pairs). Domain = discipline (primary), project.x (secondary). Computed d=fiso-fisr with pair SE sqrt(se_fiso^2+se_fisr^2); per-domain mean/median d with 95% CI, paired t and Wilcoxon, proportion |ro|>|rr| with binomial test, median relative_es and recomputed rr/ro, DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooled d. Between-domain: ANOVA/Kruskal on d and relative_es, chi-square on proportions, WLS meta-regression d~discipline weighted 1/SE^2 (classic and HC3). Sensitivity: exclude Eitam et al. (relative_es sign flip vs rr/ro) and use rr/ro. Traceability notes: relative_es does not exactly equal rr/ro (corr 0.98); `nr` used instead of `n.r` (differ in 80/86 rows). Caveat: Economics n=18.

native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Across all three domains (Social, Cognitive, Economics; equivalently Psychology and Experimental Economics projects), effect size estimates in original studies tend to be larger than in replication studies: originals exceed replications in 88.2% of Social, 82.4% of Cognitive and 83.3% of Economics study pairs (all Wilcoxon p<0.002), with mean correlation-scale shrinkage of ~0.22, 0.25 and 0.20 respectively. The tendency is most consistent and relatively strongest in Social psychology (median replication/original ratio 0.18), largest in absolute terms in Cognitive psychology, and weakest (yet still significant) in Economics, where n=18 limits power; between-domain differences are not statistically significant (meta-regression QM(2)=2.75, p=0.25).
native_result.WorkflowB: Checked data (86 pairs, no missing/duplicates, ro all positive, one relative_es sign error). Computed per-discipline and per-project paired differences ro-rr and fiso-fisr (mean, median, SD, 95% CI), proportion original>replication with exact binomial test, paired t and Wilcoxon tests; DL random-effects pooled fiso-fisr weighted by 1/(se_fiso^2+se_fisr^2) per domain and mixed-effects meta-regression with discipline moderator; sensitivity analyses with |rr| and recalculated rr/ro.

native_result.query: For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Original effect sizes exceed replication effect sizes in all three domains present (Social psychology, Cognitive psychology, Experimental Economics; equivalently both the Psychology and Economics replication projects): within each discipline the paired original-minus-replication difference is significantly positive (Fisher-z gap ~0.23-0.29, paired p<0.01) and 82-88% of studies have |r_original| > |r_replication|. The absolute gap does not differ significantly across domains (Cognitive nominally largest, 0.29 vs 0.27 Economics vs 0.23 Social; Kruskal-Wallis p=0.54), but the relative gap does: Social psychology shows the strongest shrinkage (median replication/original ratio 0.18 vs 0.65 Cognitive and 0.70 Economics, KW p=0.024), the most sign reversals (29% vs 15-17%) and the lowest replication rate (21%). Because Social originals are smallest to begin with (mean r=0.35), a similar absolute drop erases most of the effect, making the relative characterization (Social > Cognitive ≈ Economics) the more informative description of where originals are 'larger' than replications. The Economics gap is least robust (precision-weighted gap ~0.01, dominated by one large study that replicated with a larger effect; 0.14 without it).
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspected the 86x60 joined CSV: schema matched documentation; no missing values in ro, rr, fiso, fisr, se_fiso, se_fisr, relative_es, discipline, project.x/y; no duplicate studies or unmatched pairs; project.x/project.y perfectly nested within discipline (Cognitive 34, Social 34 -> Psychology/rpp; Economics 18 -> Experimental Economics/ee). Verified fiso=atanh(ro), fisr=atanh(rr), se=1/sqrt(n-3) exactly; relative_es=rr/ro in 85/86 rows (row 41 Eitam et al. had a sign error, recomputed). Flagged row 19 (Pacton/Perruchet joined to Pacton/Sobaco/Perruchet 2015) as a probable metadata mis-join, retained. Analysis (analysis.py): per-discipline and per-project paired comparisons of ro vs rr and fiso vs fisr (means, t-based 95% CIs, paired t-test, Wilcoxon), inverse-variance weighted Fisher-z difference, proportion |ro|>|rr| (Wilson CI, binomial test), proportion of sign reversals, median/IQR of recomputed rr/ro with bootstrap CI; between-domain Kruskal-Wallis/ANOVA/OLS on fiso-fisr and rr/ro, chi-square on sign reversals, WLS with precision weights, Psychology-vs-Economics Mann-Whitney; sensitivity check excluding the dominant Economics study. Outputs: per_discipline_table.csv, per_project_table.csv, analysis_output.txt.

native_result.HypoA: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.
native_result.HypoB: Economics is the domain where the majority of authors tend to be male in both original and replication studies: across 18 O/R pairs (all from the Experimental Economics project), the mean male-author ratio is 0.870 for originals and 0.837 for replications, the median is 1.0 on both sides, and 77.8% of originals and 72.2% of replications have a male-author ratio above 0.5. native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration (observed as jail residence at a 1985–1994 interview) is associated with markedly lower wealth by 1996 at every baseline wealth/income level: ever-jailed respondents hold roughly one-quarter to one-third the wealth of never-jailed peers with similar 1985 wealth (IHS gap ≈ −3 in each stratum; interactions with stratum not significant), so the relative penalty is approximately constant across income levels. In absolute dollars the gap grows with baseline wealth (median 1985→1996 growth differential ≈ $0 for the ≤$0 group, −$7.9k for the positive-low group, −$14k to −$16k for the positive-high group), while middle-wealth Black respondents show the largest increase in ending with zero wealth (61% vs 23%). Pattern holds for men alone and for alternative tercile cutpoints. Associational, not causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: Restricted to race=='black' (n=3013; 159 ever-jailed). Built baseline strata from 1985 composite wealth: primary (<=0 / positive <= $5,300 / > $5,300) and sensitivity (full-sample terciles at $134 and $10,000). Within each stratum compared ever-jailed vs never-jailed on medians for 1985/1990/1996, share with zero and negative wealth, IHS-transformed 1996 mean difference with 2000-rep bootstrap CIs, median 1985->1996 change difference with bootstrap CIs, 1st/99th-percentile-winsorized means, and Mann-Whitney tests. Fit OLS IHS(1996) ~ ever_jailed x stratum + IHS(1985) + sex with HC3 SEs plus within-stratum adjusted models; repeated everything for men only. Attempted median regression on raw dollars as a check (uninformative due to $0 conditional medians).

native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, within-group wealth inequality among white males and white females moved in the same direction with similar magnitude, and the sign depends on how zero wealth is treated. Including all observations (zeros as given), Gini rose slightly: white males 0.780→0.793, white females 0.761→0.777 (95% CIs include 0); the top-10% share was flat (0.617→0.618; 0.587→0.591); the rise came from a hollowing-out of the middle — the share with zero wealth nearly doubled (males 25.7%→43.3%, females 20.3%→42.6%), the median halved (15,601→8,900; 20,100→8,825) while the mean and p90 rose (mean 88k→132k; 100k→129k) and p90/p50 jumped from ~13 to ~37, and the share with negative wealth fell (3.7%→1.9%; 4.9%→1.9%). Restricting to positive wealth (zeros as possible masked missing), inequality fell significantly: Gini males 0.688→0.623, females 0.681→0.599; var(log) 2.99→2.50 and 3.41→2.68; top-10% share 0.537→0.478 and 0.520→0.456; the within-person panel with nonzero wealth in both years confirms this (Gini 0.693→0.630 and 0.688→0.606, medians 48k→127k and 58k→131k). The 1996 zeros are likely masked missing because 24–36% of every 1990 wealth category, including 24–26% of those above $150k, became exactly zero in 1996 (unverifiable from this file). The male–female gap in levels reversed from favoring women in 1990 (mean M−F −11,442; median −4,499; p90 −27,401) to near parity in 1996 (mean +2,956; median +75; p90 +1,890); male Gini exceeded female Gini by ~0.02 in both years (CIs include 0), and the between-sex Theil component was ≤0.1% of total inequality in both years.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows, no NaN), filtered race=='white', split by sex (M 3469, F 3630); same cohort in both years. 2) Variant A: all observations; Gini (negatives clipped to 0, plus unclipped check), top-10%/top-1% share, p90/p50, p75/p25, share zero/negative, mean, median, mean/median; paired person-level bootstrap (1000 resamples) for Gini, top10, zero share. 3) Variant B: positive wealth only, same metrics plus var(log), unpaired bootstrap. 4) Hybrid: within-person on those nonzero in both years, paired bootstrap. 5) Between-group gap M−F (mean, median, p90, Gini, zero share) with bootstrap CI; one line in 1996 dollars via CPI-U ×1.20 (external approx). 6) Theil within/between decomposition by sex on positive wealth. 7) Category transition matrix 1990→1996 (neg/zero/1-10k/10-50k/50-150k/>150k) to locate the source of the Gini rise. 8) Sensitivity: row deduplication. Script analysis/wealth_inequality.py; outputs analysis/output.txt, metrics_table.csv, bootstrap_results.json.

sub_hypo.text: From 1990 to 1996, within-group wealth inequality among white males and females increased slightly and by similar magnitudes when all observations, including zeros, were retained. sub_hypo.relations: Gini increased slightly in both sexes, with changes not statistically distinguishable from zero, while top-10% shares remained approximately constant.

native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, within-sex wealth inequality among white respondents rose modestly and similarly for males and females, driven by polarization: mean composite wealth increased (males 88,163->131,792, +49%; females 99,605->128,837, +29%) while median wealth fell (males 15,601->8,900; females 20,100->8,825) and the share with zero/negative wealth rose from ~25-29% to ~45%. Caveat: if zero-wealth observations are excluded, inequality among non-zero holders decreased (Gini -0.069 males, -0.088 females), so the direction depends on treating zeros as valid values.

native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, within-group wealth inequality among white males and white females in the NLSY79 sample stayed very high and rose slightly: Gini (incl. negatives) 0.792->0.797 for white males and 0.776->0.782 for white females (clip-at-zero 0.780->0.793 and 0.761->0.777); the p90/p50 ratio roughly tripled (13.8->37.5 males, 12.1->37.6 females), mean/median rose from 5.7/5.0 to 14.8/14.6, p90-p50 widened from ~$200k/$222k to ~$325k/$323k (nominal), and the zero-wealth share rose from 25.7%/20.3% to 43.3%/42.6%, while top-1% shares fell (23.1%->18.2%, 22.1%->18.2%) and top-10% shares were flat (~62%/59%). Inequality therefore grew via the bottom and middle of the distribution pulling apart (median fell, upper quartile rose), not via greater top concentration. White males were consistently slightly more unequal than white females (Gini gap ~+0.016 in both years, bootstrap CI includes 0) and the two sexes' inequality changes were statistically indistinguishable; the female-male wealth level gap converged from a female lead in 1990 (median +$4,499, mean +$11,442, p90 +$27,401) to near parity in 1996 (median +$75, mean +$2,956, p90 +$1,890). Gini changes lie within bootstrap noise; the p90/p50 increases are significant. Caveat: results are highly sensitive to the surge of zeros in 1996 (likely coded missing); excluding respondents with 1996==0 & 1990>0 reverses the direction (Gini 0.812->0.747 males, 0.798->0.714 females; females ahead by $29,700 at the median in 1996).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013x6); restricted to race=='white' (3,469 males, 3,630 females; no missing, balanced panel). For each sex and year (1990, 1996) computed Gini (raw incl. negatives, and clipped at 0), p25/p50/p75/p90, mean, p90/p50, p90-p50, p75-p50, top-10% and top-1% wealth shares, mean/median, zero and negative shares; computed male-minus-female gaps. Bootstrap (1,000 resamples within sex, seed 42) 95% percentile CIs for Gini, p90/p50, their 1990->1996 changes and male-female differences. Sensitivity A: drop respondents with wealth_1996==0 and wealth_1990>0 (suspected missing coded as 0). Sensitivity B: drop ever_jailed==1. Unweighted, nominal dollars.

native_result.query: How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of Socioeconomic Status and race on BA degree completion?
native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB: In NLSY79, with college entry by 1979 (highest grade >=13, age>=19) used as a proxy for BA completion, controlling for academic characteristics (age-standardized ASVAB mean; class percentile) cuts the SES effect roughly in half (AME 0.143 -> 0.061 per SD, OR 2.35 -> 1.60, -57%, bootstrap CI [-0.090,-0.075]) while it stays strongly significant, and reverses the race effects: the Black and Hispanic deficits (AME -0.052, -0.034) become advantages (+0.068, OR 1.69; +0.159, OR 3.42; p<0.001). Racial gaps in college entry are thus fully explained by measured academic achievement, whereas SES retains a substantial direct effect net of achievement; the SES effect comes from parental education and paternal occupation, not family income. Class rank adds little beyond ASVAB.

SES composite = mean of z(max parental education), z(log income, mean-imputed + indicator), z(5-level occupational status from 1970 Census codes, mean-imputed + indicator). Race dummies Black/Hispanic vs non-Black non-Hispanic. Academics: ASVAB 4 subtests z-standardized within age79, averaged; class percentile 1-(rank-1)/(size-1). Nested logits on identical sample (n=4377): M1 SES+race+female+age+sample-group; M2 +ASVAB; AME and OR compared, 500-rep bootstrap CIs on AME differences; SES components separately; race x ASVAB interaction; M3 with class percentile on subsample n=1914 with M1/M2 re-estimated. Sensitivities: complete-case and regression-imputed income, >=14 among age>=20, OLS years of schooling, 4 subtests separately, cross-sectional sample only, dorm residence 1981-85 in the younger cohort (separate sample). native_result.query: How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of Socioeconomic Status and race on BA degree completion?
native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB: Accounting for academic characteristics (ASVAB test scores, class standing) roughly halves the estimated effect of socioeconomic status on college-level attainment (SES OR per SD 2.49 -> 1.67; ~44-55% of the SES effect attributable to test scores, parental education being the most attenuated component, income having no independent effect) while the race effects reverse sign: the raw disadvantage of race codes 1 and 2 relative to Non-Black/Non-Hispanic (OR 0.46 and 0.58) is fully explained by lower SES and lower test scores, leaving a net POSITIVE conditional effect (OR 1.73 and 3.52). Class rank adds little beyond ASVAB. Pattern is consistent with mediation through academic performance, subject to timing caveats.
native_result.WorkflowB: Load data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61); set HGC=95 to missing; verify no negative sentinel codes; verify race coding via Sample ID cross-tab; construct SES composite (max parental education, 1970-Census occupation collapsed to 5 prestige levels, log income), ASVAB composite (mean of 4 re-standardized subtests), class percentile 1-(rank-1)/(size-1); outcome HGC79>=13 among age>=19; nested logits M0 (race, sex, age, sample type) -> M1 (+SES) -> M2a (+ASVAB) -> M2b (+class pct) on identical samples within tiers (Tier A n=2,659; Tier B n=1,205); ORs, AMEs, % change, KHB decomposition, 400-rep bootstrap CIs; separate SES components; race x SES interaction and race-stratified fits; robustness: OLS age-adjusted schooling progress all ages (n=6,015), ridge logit HGC>=16 age>=21 (n=1,055), drop military (n=2,159), MICE 10 imputations (n=5,427); missingness-vs-outcome/race checks.

native_result.HypoB: Using NLSY79 college-progress proxies (BA completion is not measurable in this file), the Black advantage in college progress is inversely related to socioeconomic status: Black students show a small advantage over non-Black students at low SES (some-college 11.5% vs 9.7%, RR 1.19; vs Whites RR 1.38) and mid SES (RR 1.20), but the advantage disappears and reverses to a disadvantage at high SES (30.7% vs 36.4%, RR 0.84; race x SES interaction p=0.027), with the residential-enrollment proxy showing the same declining pattern (High SES RR 0.53). Conditional on ASVAB scores the low/mid-SES Black advantage is larger (+5 to +6.5 points) but still vanishes at high SES.

Outcomes: (A) HGC79>=13 among age>=18 (primary), (B) ever dorm/frat/sorority residence 1981-86 among those observed in >=1 wave. native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: In NLSY79 (unweighted; BA completion is not directly observed, proxied by college entry = highest grade completed >=13 among respondents aged 20-22 in 1979), the Black advantage over non-Black non-Hispanic respondents in college entry is concentrated at low and especially middle parental-education SES and disappears at high SES: parental HGC<=11: Black 15.1% vs NBNH 11.8% (+3.3 pp, OR 1.33 [0.87,2.04]); parental HGC=12: 41.0% vs 24.9% (+16.1 pp, OR 2.10 [1.41,3.11]); parental HGC>=13: 52.8% vs 56.7% (-3.9 pp, OR 0.85 [0.53,1.38]). The race x SES interaction is significant (LR chi2=13.6, df=4, p=0.009; with continuous parental education the SES slope for Black respondents is 0.134 logits/grade flatter, p<0.001). Thus the Black advantage is inversely related to SES level: largest at low/middle SES, absent (point estimate slightly negative, not significant) at high SES. Controlling for ASVAB (a mediator, not SES) strengthens the Black advantage at low/middle SES while leaving the high-SES gap near zero. Caveats: proxy for college entry not BA; complete-case; parental-education missingness differs by race (2-8%) and missing cases have lower rates; income 1979 excluded from SES because it mixes own and parental income for 20-22-year-olds; no survey weights.

native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: From 1985 onwards, white (non-black non-Hispanic) NLSY79 respondents have substantially higher median family net wealth than black and Hispanic respondents, and the gap widens across waves: white median $3,500 vs black $1,600 and Hispanic $500 in 1985 (2.2x, 7x); $12,972 vs $4,800 and $1,600 in 1990 (2.7x, 8.1x); $42,600 vs $9,800 and $2,562 in 1996 (4.3x, 16.6x). Absolute gaps grow from ~$1,900/$3,000 (1985) to ~$32,800/$40,000 (1996, nominal dollars). Hispanic respondents have the lowest median wealth in every wave. The ordering and widening trend are robust to a balanced panel (n=5,739) and to restricting to the cross-sectional subsample (Sample ID 1-8); exact ratios vary (white/black 2.2-2.7x in 1985, 2.7-5.0x in 1990, 4.3-4.7x in 1996).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61). Verified cohort coding (1=Black, 2=Hispanic, 3=Non-black non-Hispanic, used as 'white' proxy) via Sample ID crosstab. Confirmed missing values are NaN (no -1..-7 codes); retained negative net wealth and topcoded values. Computed unweighted medians of Family net wealth 1985/1990/1996 by cohort on (a) per-year available cases (main), (b) balanced panel with all 3 waves, (c) cross-sectional subsample Sample ID 1-8; reported ratio of medians and absolute $ difference vs white. Missingness diagnostics: NaN % by cohort x year, by Sample ID (design dropout of IDs 9,12,15-20), and 1985 wealth of 1996 dropouts vs stayers. Percentile bootstrap (1000 reps, seed 42) 95% CIs for ratio and difference of medians on the main sample. No imputation or weighting.

native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: White (non-Black non-Hispanic) NLSY79 respondents have much higher median family net wealth than Black and Hispanic respondents in 1985, 1990 and 1996, and the gap widens over time in both absolute and ratio terms: white medians $3,500 → $12,972 → $42,600 versus Hispanic $1,600 → $4,800 → $9,800 and Black $500 → $1,600 → $2,562; white/Hispanic ratio 2.2 → 2.7 → 4.3 and white/Black ratio 7.0 → 8.1 → 16.6; absolute white–Black gap $3,000 → $40,038 and white–Hispanic gap $1,900 → $32,800. Black respondents remain lowest with the largest zero/negative-wealth share (42% in 1985, 35% in 1996 vs 19%→11% for whites). Results hold in a balanced panel and in cross-sectional samples only, and are robust to the race-code label ambiguity (documentation 1=Black/2=Hispanic vs data-consistent 1=Hispanic/2=Black), which only affects which minority group is labelled lowest.

Linearity checks: quadratic SES × race terms and quartile-dummy × race model. native_result.query: At what Socioeconomic levels is the advantage in completion rates for Black students more pronounced?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students becomes more pronounced at higher SES levels indicated by a positive interaction term SES*is_Black(coefficient:0.6271 (significant))
native_result.HypoB: After adjusting for academic resources (ASVAB composite, class percentile) plus sex and family size, Black students' advantage over White students in BA completion is absent at low socioeconomic status and emerges at middle and high SES: the adjusted Black−White gap is −0.5 pp [95% CI −1.6, 0.8] in the low SES tertile, +3.0 pp [0.7, 5.3] in the middle tertile and +1.8 pp [−1.1, 4.7] in the high tertile; in a continuous model the gap rises monotonically from +0.3 pp at SES −1 sd to +2.3 pp [0.4, 4.1] at SES +1 sd. The Black advantage is therefore more pronounced at middle-to-high SES levels and not present among low-SES students. Caveat: in raw (unadjusted) data Black students have lower completion at every SES level; the advantage exists only conditional on academic resources, and the mid-vs-high difference cannot be resolved with 236 events.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (8773 rows, 236 BA completions, no missing). Binned continuous SES into full-sample tertiles (and quintiles) and standardized it. (A) Unadjusted completion rates by race x SES bin with Wilson CIs. (B) Logistic regressions with race x SES interaction (White reference, Hispanic separate), covariates ASVAB z, class percentile z, male, family size: continuous-SES model, tertile model, and a model without class percentile (mediator check). Adjusted Black−White gap computed as difference in mean predicted P(BA) with race set to Black vs White over covariates of all respondents at each SES level. (C) Robustness: Firth-penalized logit for separation, 1000-draw race-stratified bootstrap percentile CIs, quintile bins (cells with <5 Black events flagged unreliable), Black vs all-others model. Outputs: table_raw_rates.csv, table_adjusted_gaps.csv, table_interaction_coefs.csv, analysis_output.txt.

native_result.query: Which two documentation formats are the least used for requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 10.13% (95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and 4.366% (95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) of respondents indicating so, respectively, after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: The least used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are ML Canvas (10.13% respondents, 95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) Scenarios (4.366% respondents, 95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: BDD Scenarios and ML Canvas are the two least used requirements documentation formats in ML-enabled system projects: among 194 respondents answering Q10, 2.06% (bootstrap 95% CI [0.52, 4.12]) use BDD scenarios and 7.73% (95% CI [4.12, 11.86]) use ML Canvas, significantly below the next-lowest formats Goal Models and Vision Documents (14.95% each; paired bootstrap difference vs ML Canvas 7.2 pp, 95% CI excluding 0). The ranking is robust to denominator (n=276: 1.45%/5.43%) and to restricting to Completed respondents (n=188: 2.13%/7.98%); the catch-all 'Others' category ties with ML Canvas (15 each) and 'Not documented' (15.46%) is reported separately.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded CSV (276 rows, 202 cols). Identified 12 Q10_ML_Documentation_* flag columns with values quoted/not quoted/-77. Treated -77 (82 rows, all Suspended, block-wise) as NA -> 194 respondents. For 11 named formats computed count and % quoted; bootstrap with B=10000 respondent resamples (numpy seed 42), percentile 2.5/97.5 CI; Wilson CI as control; paired bootstrap differences between bottom formats and third-lowest. Sensitivities: n=276 (-77 as not quoted), Completed-only (n=188), Others included. Reported Not_Documented and Others separately. Documented non-reproducibility of the question's stated percentages across denominators tried (194, 276, 164, 386, 416) and showed CI-of-bootstrap-mean as alternative narrow-interval interpretation.

The groups differ in dynamics: in developing/LMC countries, increases in education expenditure share coincide with slightly faster per-capita income growth (first-difference coefficient ~+0.02, p~0.01-0.03; ~0 in a dynamic model), whereas in Sub-Saharan Africa the association is negative in both levels (r=-0.97, n=5) and changes (pooled interaction -0.074, p<0.001). Thus the education-expenditure/per-capita-income link appears weaker (more negative) in Sub-Saharan Africa than in developing countries. Secondary enrollment, primary enrollment and labor force participation are the strongest positive level correlates of income in LMC, and exports growth is the strongest correlate of income growth. Results are associations subject to denominator effects (edu as % of GNI), reverse causality, group overlap, and the 5-observation SSA outcome.

native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference, proxied by 1989 saving behaviour (not putting money into savings / drawing savings down rather than saving), is associated with higher BMI in NLSY79 (about +0.15 to +0.22 BMI units per proxy step; +0.4 to +0.5 units for non-savers/withdrawers vs savers) after controlling for sex, race, age, own and parental education, family income, net wealth, ASVAB scores and incarceration. native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 cohort, higher time preference — proxied by impatient savings behaviour in 1989 (taking money out of savings or having no savings, versus putting money into savings) — is associated with higher BMI: BMI 1989 is about 0.4 units higher for TOOK OUT / NO CHANGE and about 0.9 units higher for NO SAVINGS relative to savers (binary impatient indicator +0.44 BMI, 95% CI 0.22–0.65), controlling for sex, age, race/ethnicity, education (highest grade completed), family size, sample type, log family income 1989 and net family wealth 1990. The association holds for lagged BMI 1992 (+0.44), for BMI change 1981→1989 (+0.27), with incarceration (jail residence) and ASVAB/class rank added as controls, and under imputation of missing controls; it is stronger among women than men. Academic-performance proxies point the same way (higher ASVAB and class rank → lower BMI), while incarceration does not (jail → lower BMI). The relationship is observational and modest in size (≈0.1–0.2 SD of BMI) and should be read as an association consistent with, not proof of, a causal effect of time preference on BMI.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61). Decoded height 1981 (FFII) and height 1985 (inches); treated weight as pounds (assumption; doc says kg; BMI>=30 share 12.7% in 1989 passes sanity check); dropped weight code 996 and implausible values; BMI=703*lb/in^2 for 1981, 1989, 1992. 2) Exposure: savings 1989 category (PUT_IN ref / NO_CHANGE / TOOK_OUT / NO_SAVINGS), binary impatient = TOOK_OUT|NO_SAVINGS, supplementary asinh(net flow) winsorised 1/99. Secondary proxies: jail residence any year 1981-89, ASVAB mean z, class-rank percentile. 3) Samples: BMI89 n=10,438 -> +savings 10,410 -> +base controls 10,274 (core) -> +income89 & wealth90 7,309 (full). native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference, proxied by 1989 savings behavior (having no savings or withdrawing from savings instead of depositing), is associated with higher BMI in NLSY79: no-savings +0.95 kg/m2 crude and +0.66 kg/m2 (95% CI 0.29-1.02) after controlling for sex, race/ethnicity, age, sample type, 1989 income, 1985 net wealth, 1979 family income, education, ASVAB, class rank, parental education, father's occupation at 14, family size and incarceration; withdrawing +0.59 crude / +0.44 adjusted. Obesity OR 1.63 crude / 1.30 adjusted for no savings. The association survives income and wealth controls (so is not merely poverty), is stronger among women, replicates for BMI 1992, but attenuates when adjusting for 1981 BMI, so causality is not established.
