native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference, proxied by 1989 savings behavior (taking money out of savings or having no savings rather than adding to savings), is associated with modestly higher subsequent BMI: each step on a 0-2 impatience scale corresponds to about +0.2 to +0.5 kg/m2 in 1992 BMI (0.51 unadjusted; ~0.20-0.22 after controlling sex, age, race, parental education, family income, father's occupation, ASVAB, class rank, 1989 income, 1985 wealth and 1981 baseline BMI; p<0.05), roughly 4-10% of a BMI SD. Both 'took money out' and 'no savings' groups show higher BMI than 'put money in' (+0.4-0.5 in the large adjusted model), and the pattern replicates with continuous net savings and 1985-1990 wealth change. The association is small, directionally consistent across sensitivity analyses (incarceration, military sample, missing-indicator, IPW), weaker for 1989 same-year BMI with baseline control and for women, and is observational rather than causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: Clean NLSY79 variables (height 1985/1981 feet-inch conversion; weight treated as pounds; BMI=703*lb/in^2 clipped 12-70; remove codes 996, 8192797, 9999996, income top-codes). OLS with HC1 SE for BMI 1992 (primary), BMI 1989, and BMI changes, stepwise covariates incl. baseline BMI 1981; exclude incarcerated (residence code 5) in main; sensitivity: include jailed + ever_jail, exclude military, by sex, obesity logit, missing-indicator, IPW for 1992 attrition; attrition comparison table.

sub_hypo.text: Higher time preference, proxied by taking money out of savings or having no savings rather than adding to savings in 1989, is associated with modestly higher subsequent BMI in 1992. Each step on a 0–2 impatience scale corresponds to approximately 0.51 kg/m² higher BMI unadjusted and 0.20–0.22 kg/m² higher BMI after adjustment (p<0.05), approximately 4–10% of a BMI standard deviation. In the large adjusted model, both taking money out and having no savings are associated with approximately 0.4–0.5 kg/m² higher BMI than putting money in. The pattern replicates using continuous net savings and 1985–1990 wealth change, remains directionally consistent across sensitivity analyses, and is weaker for women and for same-year 1989 BMI with baseline BMI control. The association is observational, not causal.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents with cleaned savings, anthropometric and covariate data; the main analysis excludes incarcerated respondents identified by residence code 5. Savings behavior is measured in 1989 and primary BMI in 1992, with secondary analyses of 1989 BMI and BMI changes. BMI is calculated as 703 × weight in pounds / height in inches squared, using converted 1985/1981 heights and clipping BMI to 12–70. Invalid codes and income top-codes are removed. Sensitivity analyses include incarcerated respondents with an ever-jailed control, exclude the military sample, stratify by sex, use missing indicators and inverse-probability weighting for 1992 attrition, and examine obesity with logistic regression.

native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference, proxied by taking money out of savings or having no savings (vs. adding to savings) in 1989, is associated with higher BMI in NLSY79: adjusted +0.48 BMI units (95% CI 0.21-0.74) for the high-time-preference group in 1989, with a monotone gradient (no change +0.28, took out +0.43, no savings +0.79 vs put more in), robust to adding income and wealth (+0.46), present for BMI 1992 (+0.43), stronger in women (+0.70) than men (+0.21, n.s.), and attenuated when conditioning on 1981 baseline BMI (+0.18). This is an association, not a causal estimate.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61). Documented departure from data dictionary: weights treated as pounds and Height 1981 decoded from feet*100+inches (kg assumption gives impossible median BMI 53.5; lb gives 24.3; height81/85 corr 0.934). BMI = 703*lb/in^2 using 1985 height (fallback 1981), sentinel codes (996 weight, savings amounts >=1e6, grade 95) set missing, BMI restricted to 12-70. Exposure: 4-category 1989 savings behavior (ref put more in) and binary high time preference (took out OR no savings); secondary IHS net saving and net saving/income. Outcomes: BMI 1989 (primary), BMI 1992, BMI conditional on 1981 BMI, obesity (BMI>=30) logit. Nested OLS with HC1 robust SE: M1 demographics; M2 + education, parental education, father occupation, family size/income 1979, ASVAB, class rank, conviction/sentencing (missing->0 + indicator), jail residence; M3 + IHS income 1989 (top-code flag) and IHS net wealth 1990. Sensitivities: exclude no-savings category, sample-type indicators, cross-sectional subsample only, median regression, MICE imputation of covariates (10 imputations), sex stratification and interaction. Attrition comparison of 1989 respondents vs non-respondents on 1979/1981 characteristics.
